lines.en: If I still talk about water, it is because here there is water that does not freeze even in the Great Cold.

lines.en: I will start with the conclusion. Ōtsu was not a town where journeys ended, but a town of people whose journeys went on.

lines.en: That is today's claim. There are three parts: first Lake Biwa, then the water of Hashirii, and finally the rest of the road to Kyoto.

lines.en: It is so wide that walking around it takes a good ten days. And it is old: it is said to have been born four million years ago.

lines.en: Even in the Great Cold, this lake never freezes over completely. There is too much water for it to chill all the way through.

lines.en: The inns of Ōtsu stood on a slope looking down over this lake. People coming from the east knew here that Kyoto was near.

lines.en: The strange thing is its temperature. Even on a Great Cold morning, when you put your hand in, it feels lukewarm rather than cold.

lines.en: So even when it is two degrees outside, the water comes up at fifteen degrees. It could not freeze even if it wanted to, so to speak.

lines.en: Hashirii mochi, too, is made with this water: sweet bean paste wrapped in soft mochi, in a shape you can eat while holding it in your hand.

items.recapEn: A lecture on Ōtsu, the last post town: Lake Biwa is ancient and never freezes over; the Hashirii spring stays near fifteen degrees because groundwater follows the soil, so travellers drank standing before the Ōsaka climb; seventy-one inns held one-night guests. Thesis: Ōtsu was a town for people continuing their journey, where the road's end was also a beginning.

items.recapEn: On the last night the three return to the Hashirii spring with a borrowed flashlight and Ken tastes the fifteen-degree water. At the inn Tanaka-san's watch and the wall clock agree for the first time because Ken reset the clock; Tanaka-san concedes only a possibility. At dawn the cat sits on Ken's boots and Hana, for once, plays the doubter.
